title: Lamp, Telephone, Mango: Remembering Arpita Singh and How She Saw the World Around Her

Photo: Samar Jodha Advertisement Arpita Singh died in Delhi on Monday, at 89. Gallerist Shireen Gandhy, whose father's Delhi gallery, Kunika Chemould, held Arpita's first solo show in 1972, wrote that she has gone "taking a small piece of our hearts with her".
 I met her and her husband Paramjit Singh, the painter, in the mid-90s, before the internet, when the Art Today gallery was opening in Connaught Place. Aman Nath curated its inaugural show, Delhi artists each with the painting they would want to be remembered by for posterity, as Aman framed it, and I was commissioned to photograph the works and the painters for the catalogue. We started at Garhi, the Lalit Kala Akademi studios in East of Kailash, and I followed their car back to their home to shoot a painting. More than 30 years later, I honestly can't say whether it was hers or Paramjit's, or which one.
 I was in my 20s, and I had never imagined I would be in a home like that, two painters living and working under one roof, with art all around, and I felt honoured just to be there. Paramjit, who is from Amritsar, has spent more than six decades painting landscapes.
 Meanwhile, she was born in 1937 in Baranagar, near Calcutta, came to Delhi with her family in 1946, just before Partition, and studied at the Delhi Polytechnic, where she met Paramjit, whom she married in 1962. After 1959, she worked as a textile designer at the Weavers' Service Centre, and you can see it in her painting all her life, the borders around her canvases, the small motifs repeated across the surface. For most of the 70s, she put colour and the figure away and worked in ink on paper, lines, grids and dots, which she later compared to practising handwriting.
 On that Art Today shoot I also photographed the work of Anjolie Ela Menon and Krishen Khanna, among others. I was a young photographer just starting out in the city, with no background in painting, and this part of the art community was a whole new discovery for me, women and men who were clearly coming from deep experiences of the post-Partition years.
 Advertisement 
 It was still an art world run by men. The Progressive Artists' Group, Husain, Souza, Raza, had set the terms after Independence, and the few women who painted were treated as exceptions. A few years before, Arpita had taken her work around the country with three other women painters, Nalini Malani, Nilima Sheikh and Madhvi Parekh, in ‘Through the Looking Glass’, often called the first all-women exhibition in India.
 When the figure came back in her work, it was mostly a woman, middle-aged, heavy, often undressed, painted as she was, not idealised, with teapots, pillows and flowers around her, and often someone she knew, a friend, a neighbour, her own mother. "I make women because that form I know very well," she once said. She never called her work feminist. In a 2003 conversation, Nilima Sheikh asked her whether women artists, never having staked their ideologies on art movements, were less bound by their grammar, and she replied, "Being unmindful of them is what gives us our freedom." The canvases were full of women anyway, painted from her own life.
 Advertisement 
 The politics came from the newspaper she read every day, and from what she and Paramjit lived through in Delhi, the Emergency and the killing of Sikhs in 1984. Shireen wrote that Arpita called herself "non-political" but had "the sharpest metaphorical responses". After 1984, guns, knives and soldiers started turning up on her canvases, among the flowers, cars and aeroplanes. In ‘Devi Pistol Wali’, from 1990, the goddess holds a pistol. ‘My Mother’ was painted after the Bombay riots of 1992-93 that followed the demolition of the Babri Masjid. In it, most of the canvas is taken up by the violence, and in one corner is an old woman in white, who, she told the curator Tamsin Hong, stands exactly as her own mother once stood greeting a nephew at the door. The riots and her mother are on the same canvas. As someone who works with a camera, where you pick one frame and leave the rest outside it, I find that very hard to do.
 And there is a lot of play in it. Her men hold bouquets as well as guns, the women float above the ground, and the canvases are labelled like a school chart – LAMP, TELEPHONE, MANGO. Her friend Nilima Sheikh has said Arpita talked about violence and injustice "using the language of play".
 Advertisement 
 In India, Arpita had long been counted among the leading painters of her generation, while the Padma Bhushan came in 2011. In 2019, the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art gave her a first retrospective, ‘Submergence: In the Midst of Here and There’, curated by Roobina Karode. Kiran Nadar, one of the country's foremost collectors, said at the time, "I hesitate to call Arpita Singh ‘a woman painter.’ She is quite simply one of the great modernists of our time."
 Advertisement 
 Last year, at 87, the Serpentine in London gave her a solo show.
 I took this portrait of her (the main image) only a month ago, at a dinner at the home of Renu Modi of Gallery Espace, where over the years I have met many artists of her generation, Arpita among them.
 Samar Jodha is a transdisciplinary artist and TED speaker whose practice spans South Asia, West Asia and East Africa.
